Gold, which had topped 3,636.67, is back below it this morning.

As of 06:56 on Nov 24, XS's MT5 (XAUUSDs) is at 3,633.45. Today's daily high is 3,689.71, which briefly exceeded the previous day's high of 3,636.67. On TradingView, the first thing I look at is where the previous day's high and the 4-hour SMA20 (3,639.23) are close together - I treat the daily level and the 4H moving average as one band.

Looking back at yesterday's no-trade situation: Nov 23 07:00 at 3,534.69, near last week's low of 3,502.78. In my verification, I wouldn't mark a rebound just because it's near a low; I record which level it manages to clear on the way back up. This morning I'll do that check around the previous day's high.

[If it returns upward] Whether a 4H bar closes above 3,639.23. If it does, I watch how far the pullback continues between the round number 3,650.00 and today's high 3,689.71. The 4H SMA20 is below the SMA50 (3,783.12), so I note the direction of longer timeframes separately.

[If it moves away downward] If the rebound stalls below the band, first the reaction at 3,600.00. If the decline continues there, I watch the band near today's open 3,553.93 and low 3,553.00. If it breaks below, the next observation is where the decline stops before 3,502.78, which is both last week's low and the 4H trough.

What I note separately in my verification memo: whether the wick went beyond the band, and which side the 4H close stayed on. I don't judge by the morning price alone; I check after the bar is confirmed. Trade at your own judgment.

I share these level verification memos in the open chat "Hide Gold FX Study Group" in my profile.

[Must-read] 6 math checks so you don't get fooled by MT5 backtests of the "free gold EAs" circulating on X

People keep losing 1-2 million yen on EAs handed out free on condition of opening an account via an IB (introducing broker). When spotting dubious reports, ignore the flashy net profit and check just these 6 points.

1. Is the header above "Currency: JPY" cropped out? The header shows broker name, spread, external commission (about $7 round trip per lot on a Raw account) and period. If it is trimmed, the test was very often run in a commission-free, favorable environment.

2. Check the tick count and "OnTester result". If ticks / bars is exactly 4.0x, it is a simplified 1-minute OHLC simulation, not real ticks. A non-zero "OnTester result" indicates over-optimization (curve fitting) to that period only.

3. Look at "equity relative drawdown" and "maximum consecutive loss amount", not the "max DD x%" in the text. Dividing by the larger balance after late profits makes "DD 18%" look small. If the starting balance is 1M yen and max DD is 1.5M yen, an early drawdown means instant stop-out.

4. Abnormal "Z-Score" and trade counts. With an extremely negative Z-Score (-100 or lower) and 100-200+ max consecutive wins/losses, the structure is holding about 200 positions of 0.01 lot (effectively 2 lots) in a clump and closing them all at once. If the expected gain per trade is only a few hundred yen, commissions and slippage on a real account wipe out the profit, leaving only the distributor's IB rewards (ultra high-turnover lots).

5. The "backtesting prohibited to protect the logic" trap. In MQL5, allowing the tester only for a verified account number (ACCOUNT_LOGIN) takes a few lines. Blocking pre-verification while saying "if you want to check, deposit and run it on a live account" is extremely dangerous.

6. Do they reply instantly to "account opening" questions but completely ignore questions about numbers and specs? Accounts that answer IB-funnel comments like "Can I get it for free?" within minutes but never answer technical questions such as "Is the external commission/relative DD consistent?" or "Show the report with header", and quietly rewrite inconvenient figures behind the scenes, deserve caution.

A system with a real edge has no need to hide its code skeleton, its verification tests or the live-account logs of losing days. Before putting in your funds, stop and check what's behind the numbers.

[Sharing the lot calculator I've been using lately ♪]

When trading off the charts every day, I think everyone finds lot calculation a hassle.

I've shared a free calculator site in the past, in both my YouTube videos and PDF materials ("I calculate with this site"), but it has drawbacks:

* Every calculation takes time.
* Typing in entry and stop-loss values each time is tedious.
* A typo can throw the lot size off and cause an unexpected loss.
* So you worry whether it's really correct and have to double-check.

When the scenario has been clear for hours and there is time before entry it's fine, but when you want to enter right away you get flustered, which makes mistakes more likely - a vicious circle. With no time before entry and a tedious calculation, you can't focus on chart analysis and misjudgments become more likely.

After searching around I found a very handy tool and I'm using it now: "Easy Order" (links to my blog article).
https://t.co/rIqMKqNjE0…

As explained in the blog, you don't type in numbers - you just drag three horizontal lines (entry, stop-loss, take-profit) up and down on MT4 and it automatically calculates the appropriate lot size. Market, limit and stop orders can be placed with one click, and the risk-reward ratio is displayed automatically. It removes the stress and worry of lot and risk-reward calculations.

It works with overseas FX brokers such as XM, which I use, and also with CFDs and crypto, so there is no need to split tools by asset class.

It isn't free, but at 4,500 yen it's quite reasonable. Many people who trade the same way as me already use this tool.
https://t.co/rIqMKqNjE0…

It frees you from all the hassle of lot calculation so you can concentrate on chart analysis. I recommend it to anyone who struggles with lot or risk-reward calculations - quietly sharing it on the last night of the long weekend. 😁
